title: Hearth & Harvest Village Bakery
setting: The stone-arched hearth kitchen, flour pantry, and cobblestone delivery lanes of Oakhaven Village, where wood-fired deck ovens operate from dawn to dusk.

sources.title: The Perfect Loaf - Sourdough Hydration Guide
King Arthur Baking - Sourdough Baking with Steam
King Arthur Baking - How to Store Bread

rules: Baker's percentages standardize all ingredient weights relative to total flour weight at 100%.
Proper gluten network formation requires adequate hydration and mechanical or autolyse agitation.
Steam must be retained during early baking to delay crust gelatinization, enabling oven spring before dry baking.
Gluten-containing and gluten-free items must maintain strict segregation to prevent cross-contamination.
Bread crumb staling accelerates fastest at refrigerator temperatures between 2°C and 6°C due to retrogradation.
assumptions: The village bakery operates a heavy stone deck oven heated with seasoned hardwood and a steam-injection chamber.
Flour varieties are sourced locally from the village watermill with documented protein content.
Deliveries are executed via handcart or wicker pack lined with natural linen to preserve crust crispness.

tasks.title: Country Loaf Dough Formulation
tasks.summary: Calculate and scale the flour, water, and salt quantities to achieve an open crumb and balanced salinity in an artisanal sourdough country loaf.
tasks.mechanic_rationale: Ingredient scaling directly dictates dough hydration and salt concentration, which mathematically control gluten structure, fermentation kinetics, and crust color.
tasks.aim: Balance dough hydration and salinity to achieve an open, aerated crumb structure without slack spreading.

optima.rationale: A standard village hearth banneton is sized precisely for a 500 g flour base.
Standard artisan bread dough requires exactly 2.0% salt relative to flour (10 g salt per 500 g flour) to regulate yeast fermentation and tighten gluten.
A classic country boule achieves an open crumb and shape stability at 72% to 76% hydration.

heuristic.too_low: The batch volume is too meager for the proofing baskets, resulting in a squat loaf.
heuristic.too_high: The dough overflows the banneton and spills over the hearth stones.
heuristic.rationale: Bannetons and oven deck allocations require consistent base dough volumes.

heuristic.too_low: The crumb lacks structural resilience and the flavor is flat and bland.
heuristic.too_high: The yeast fermentation is stunted, leaving the bread pale, dense, and unpleasantly salty.
heuristic.rationale: Salt stabilizes gluten bonding and curbs proteolytic enzymatic activity.

heuristic.too_low: The dough feels stiff and tight, producing a compact sandwich crumb rather than an open artisan interior.
heuristic.too_high: The dough lacks sufficient surface tension and puddles into a flat disc upon scoring.
heuristic.rationale: Hydration determines starch swelling, enzymatic access, and gluten extensibility.

caveats: Flour ambient moisture and protein content change throughout the seasons, altering water absorption capacity.
Salt should be dissolved or integrated evenly to avoid localized yeast inhibition.
problems: Extremely wet dough sticking tenaciously to hands and bench scrapers without building an outer skin.
Under-salted dough fermenting unpredictably fast and collapsing during scoring.

tasks.title: Deck Oven Crust & Bake Timing
tasks.summary: Operate the deck oven steam valve and bake duration to ensure full loaf expansion before setting a deep caramelized crust.
tasks.mechanic_rationale: Baking requires sequential, time-critical interventions: maintaining high-humidity steam while the loaf expands, then venting the flue for dry Maillard browning.
tasks.aim: Trap steam long enough for maximum oven spring, then vent and bake until the crust reaches deep mahogany caramelization.

optima.rationale: Steam must surround the loaf for the first 18 to 22 minutes to prevent premature crust setting and maximize loaf expansion.
After venting steam, artisan loaves require 20 to 24 minutes of dry heat at deck temperature to gelatinize starches, drive off interior moisture, and develop blistered, mahogany crusts.

heuristic.too_low: The crust formed prematurely, strangling the loaf ear and producing a dull, thick rind.
heuristic.too_high: The crust remained rubbery and waterlogged, causing the loaf walls to collapse inward upon cooling.
heuristic.rationale: Steam keeps the outer dough extensible and starches moist during early thermal expansion.

heuristic.too_low: The crumb retains a gummy raw core and the crust turns soggy within an hour of resting.
heuristic.too_high: The outer crust is scorched and bitter, masking the delicate fermented aromas of the crumb.
heuristic.rationale: Dry baking drives core temperature past 98°C and creates Maillard browning.

caveats: Opening the oven door repeatedly releases radiant stone heat and vents humidity prematurely.
Darker crusts seal in moisture, keeping the interior tender while the shell stays crisp.
problems: Pale, leathery crust with torn wild ruptures instead of clean scored expansion.
Sunken bottom crust caused by thermal shock from premature venting.

tasks.title: Mill Sack Grain & Flour Sorting
tasks.summary: Inspect and sort fresh mill deliveries into the proper storage bins based on gluten potential, milling extraction, and dietary safety.
tasks.mechanic_rationale: Bakers must accurately route flours according to protein concentration and allergen status to avoid recipe failures or allergen cross-contact.
tasks.aim: Route milled flours into Bread Flour, Pastry Flour, or Gluten-Free Specialty bins without cross-contamination.

sort_items.label: Hard Red Winter Wheat (13.5% Protein)
sort_items.feedback: Hard winter wheat contains high protein necessary for strong gluten networks in hearth breads.

sort_items.label: Soft White Wheat (8.5% Protein)
sort_items.feedback: Soft low-protein wheat belongs in the pastry bin to yield tender biscuits and cakes.

sort_items.label: Stoneground Buckwheat Groat Flour
sort_items.feedback: Buckwheat is a pseudocereal containing zero gluten proteins, requiring dedicated allergen isolation.

sort_items.label: High-Extraction Durum Semolina (14% Protein)
sort_items.feedback: Durum has tenacious protein structure ideal for rustic loaves and hearth breads.

sort_items.label: Chlorinated Cake Flour (7.5% Protein)
sort_items.feedback: Weak gluten and fine milling make this suited exclusively for delicate, aerated pastries.

sort_items.label: Finely Milled Sweet White Rice Flour
sort_items.feedback: Rice flour lacks prolamins and must be kept in the sealed gluten-free bin to avoid cross-contact.

caveats: Protein percentage is not synonymous with gluten quality; damaged starches also skew dough absorption.
Airborne flour dust can contaminate open gluten-free bins in communal storage spaces.
problems: Baking sandwich cakes with strong bread flour results in a tough, rubbery crumb.
Accidental contamination of gluten-free bins triggers severe allergen exposure.

tasks.title: Village Morning Bread Delivery
tasks.summary: Pack and transport fresh morning breads across Oakhaven Village, observing ventilation and thermal preservation protocols.
tasks.mechanic_rationale: Artisan breads undergo crumb structure stabilization during transport, demanding distinct ventilation, stacking, and moisture controls per loaf variety.
tasks.aim: Deliver hot and fragile breads to the village destinations without softening crisp crusts or crushing delicate crumb.

orders.item: Crusty Dark Rye Boules (Fresh from Oven)
orders.note: Transport in open-slat wooden crates lined with breathable linen; sealing in bags will trap steam and turn the crust soggy.
Shield completely from damp river mist with wax-paper wraps; high fat crumb softens rapidly if exposed to damp air.
Heavy loaves must rest on the bottom rack; keep vertical air gaps between loaves to preserve side blister crusts.
Top-tier load only; fragile crumb structure will collapse if stacked beneath dense sourdough loaves.

caveats: Hot bread continues to expel steam for up to two hours post-bake; impermeable wrapping is fatal to crust crispness.
Stacking warm loaves causes moisture from the bottom loaf to condense into the base of the loaf above.
problems: Tavern rye arriving with wrinkled, leathery crusts due to plastic transport wraps.
Flattened rolls resulting from improper crate stacking weight distribution.

tasks.title: Village Bakery Counter Consultation
tasks.summary: Advise village patrons on crumb preservation, sourdough digestion, and dietary accommodations over the bakery counter.
tasks.mechanic_rationale: Counter service requires nuanced food science knowledge to prevent food waste, demystify fermentation, and protect patrons with celiac disease.
tasks.aim: Provide accurate bread preservation guidance and uphold strict allergen safety advice.

dialogue.npc_line: My sourdough boule loses its crispness by day two! I was thinking of keeping it in my cold cellar larder or ice chest. Will that keep it fresh longer?

options.text: Refrigeration actually accelerates starch retrogradation, making bread go stale up to six times faster. Store it cut-side down on a wooden board or in a breathable paper bag at room temperature.
options.feedback: Scientifically accurate; retrogradation occurs fastest near refrigeration temperatures (2°C - 6°C).

options.text: Yes, sealing it tightly in an airtight glass container in the cold cellar keeps moisture trapped inside the crust.
options.feedback: Trapping moisture makes the crust rubbery and encourages rapid mold growth in humid conditions.

options.text: Just slice it all up now and leave the slices open on the kitchen table so they stay dry.
options.feedback: Pre-slicing completely dries out the crumb within a few hours.

dialogue.npc_line: My niece has medically diagnosed celiac disease. Since your sourdough undergoes a long 36-hour wild yeast fermentation, that means the gluten is completely broken down and safe for her, right?

options.text: Yes, long sourdough fermentation digests 100% of the gluten proteins, so anyone with celiac disease can eat our wheat loaves without worry!
options.feedback: Dangerous falsehood. Fermentation reduces some gluten fragments, but wheat sourdough remains toxic to individuals with celiac disease.

options.text: While long fermentation partially hydrolyzes some gluten, residual gluten peptides remain far above safety limits. She must strictly avoid all wheat, barley, and rye breads.
options.feedback: Essential allergen safety communication that protects celiac customers from life-threatening intestinal damage.

options.text: She can eat the crust because the oven heat burns off all the proteins, but she should avoid the inner crumb.
options.feedback: Nonsensical advice that endangers the customer's health.

dialogue.npc_line: I love a tangy, sour profile in my morning bread, but last week's batch tasted very mild. How do your bakers naturally coax that rich tang out of the starter?

options.text: We just dump half a cup of village cider vinegar directly into the mixer during the final stretch and fold.
options.feedback: Vinegar mimics acidity artificially but destroys authentic wild fermentation complexity.

options.text: A long, cold retarding phase in the dough proof allows lactic and acetic acid bacteria to produce complex acids while yeast activity slows down.
options.feedback: Accurately reflects the microbiology of sourdough: cool temperatures favor bacterial acid production over yeast gas production.

options.text: We shorten the bulk proofing time to under an hour so the wild yeasts don't consume all the sugar.
options.feedback: Shortening proofing produces under-fermented, sweet, and bland dough with no acidity.

caveats: Never conflate mild wheat sensitivity with celiac disease; always err on the side of strict allergen safety.
Customer satisfaction relies on clear, demystified explanations of starch chemistry and fermentation.
problems: Customers refrigerating high-end loaves and complaining about premature crumb staling.
Misunderstandings regarding sourdough fermentation causing allergen safety violations.

reasoning_traces.thought: Selected the cozy village setting of Oakhaven Hearth Bakery with 5 distinct tasks across all 5 mechanics: mix, timing, sort, deliver, converse.
Designed the mix task around baker's percentages with strong flour, spring water, and fine sea salt, featuring derived hydration percentage with realistic artisan ranges.
Designed the timing task around the critical two-stage bake cycle: steam retention for loaf expansion, followed by dry venting for Maillard crust development.
Structured grain sorting to categorize flours into high-gluten, low-gluten, and gluten-free bins based on real protein fractions and allergen cross-contact concerns.
Crafted delivery and counter dialogue tasks that address moisture control during hot bread transport, retrogradation in bread storage, and critical celiac allergen warnings.
